synthesis.headline: The late-summer dipole re-amplifies: a cold-core cutoff reforms over the Great Lakes and swings the severe stream toward the Northeast — but the ensembles cast it as a departing guest while the Southwest heat ridge reloads across the south
synthesis.narrative:
After yesterday's flattening toward progressive flow, the eastern half of the pattern has re-amplified. The 12Z 500 mb analysis shows a cold-core cutoff low over the upper Midwest and Great Lakes — closed 552-558 dam contours with a cold temperature core collocated with the height minimum — separated from the main westerlies and paired with the entrenched Desert Southwest/Great Basin ridge near 594 dam, a 35-40 dam couplet. The DuPage analysis reads this as blocked rather than progressive, and the geometry fits a self-retaining system that will pivot in place rather than translate quickly downstream. The important qualifier is that this is a transient re-amplification of the eastern trough, not the onset of a durable block: the ensemble pair (below) has the trough lifting northeast into Canada over the next one to two weeks while the ridge reloads and expands warmth across the south. Compared with yesterday's near-neutral, un-closed trough, today is a genuine step back toward amplitude on the eastern flank — but a temporary one.

Today's centers of action divide between the ridge and its periphery, the same split Tlaloc has tracked all week. The durable, dangerous element is the heat: WPC carries highs of 100-115 F across the Southwest and south-central U.S. with Major-to-Extreme HeatRisk over Texas and the Southwest through Thursday and poor overnight recovery — suppression and baking driven by midlevel subsidence and warming, a strengthened cap, and dry-air entrainment under the ridge, not by the modest 1017-1018 mb surface highs beneath it. The severe stream rings the cutoff: SPC's Day 1 Slight Risk runs from the southern Great Lakes and Midwest through the central/southern High Plains to the Ozarks, Mid-South, and Lower Mississippi Valley, with damaging winds the primary threat and large hail favored in the central High Plains upslope regime. The surface pattern supports this best where Gulf dewpoints in the mid-to-upper 70s meet the cold front draped from a 1006 mb northern-Rockies/Plains low across the central Plains and mid-South. The Day 2 outlook shows the threat pivoting downstream on Thursday: an embedded shortwave rotating around the Great Lakes trough carries a Slight Risk from Lake Erie into the Northeast (VT/NH, eastern New York), while a conditional big-hail/wind threat lingers over the central High Plains even as rising heights on the eastward-shifting ridge work to cap it. Elsewhere, a slow Southeast boundary prolongs heavy rain, and monsoon moisture keeps daily high-terrain convection going over the Southwest and Rockies. The other genuinely active surface feature is Pacific: a roughly 1000 mb coastal low off the Pacific Northwest with a cold front sweeping down the California/Nevada coast, where the tightest gradient on the map compresses into British Columbia.

The upper structure ties it together. The Air Mass RGB shows a broad, dry orange-red expanse over the central Plains, Texas, and northern Mexico that is ridge-top subsidence, not a stratospheric signature, while a compact reddish streamer curls cyclonically from the upper Midwest toward the Tennessee Valley on the cutoff's eastern flank; the abrupt color transition from Iowa-Illinois into the central Appalachians marks the implied jet corridor steering the convection. Over Canada the full-disk imagery shows a sharp airmass boundary arching from the northern Prairies into Quebec and Labrador — the polar jet corridor separating cold, dry air to the north — and a cyclonically curving orange-red streamer off the western Canadian coast into the Gulf of Alaska that, on the cyclonic flank of a trough, is a credible high-PV/stratospheric-intrusion signature tied to the Pacific Northwest/BC trough. On the regime question, the ensemble pair is the test and it points the same direction as yesterday. The 6-10 day (Aug 31-Sep 4) has the ridge at 588 dam across the central and eastern CONUS, a closed low over the northwestern Canadian interior (about -90 m), and the zero-anomaly line along the U.S.-Canada border. The 8-14 day (Sep 2-8) retreats that trough northeast to the Arctic Archipelago/Baffin region while the ridge core settles over the Desert Southwest and northern Mexico (588 dam) with a broad +6 dam or greater positive anomaly across the central and southern CONUS. Read together, the positive anomaly holds and broadens across the south while the northern trough migrates from northwestern Canada to the Arctic — geographic contraction and an eastward/southward reload, not a collapse. Today's Great Lakes cutoff lifts out into that departing northern stream; the ridge does not vanish, it expands. The Day 2 note that the ridge shifts east toward the Plains is the first frame of that reload.
synthesis.climate_context: This is peak-summer North America close to the seasonal script: the North American Monsoon is active and feeding daily high-terrain convection across the Southwest and Rockies, and severe weather is expressed as ridge-periphery, northern-stream storms and frontal supercells rather than deep-Plains outbreaks. The ENSO backdrop is a decisively developing warm state — the ONI has climbed from weak La Niña in late 2025 through neutral in spring to roughly +1.4 C by late spring/early summer 2026, a clear trend toward at least a moderate El Niño. That configuration typically favors an active eastern Pacific while shear and dry air suppress the Atlantic, and even as the basin approaches its early-September climatological peak the tropics fit the split neatly: Tropical Storms Lala and Iselle plus a near-certain EP93 south of Mexico (80-90%), a developing broad low east-southeast of Hawaii, and two more candidate areas against only a low-end, deteriorating Atlantic wave (AL96, 60% but fading by the weekend). Summer teleconnection indices are weak, lagging cross-checks on the height field rather than drivers of it: a sharply negative NAO (-1.28) and a weakly negative, falling PNA are loosely consistent with sluggish Atlantic flow and slower eastward progression, but they should be read as no more than a nod to the story the height and PV fields already tell.
synthesis.regional_notes: SPC has no active mesoscale discussions, so severe risk stands at outlook level, shifting from the Great Lakes/High Plains/Mid-South today into the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast on Thursday, with a conditional 2-inch-hail/75-mph threat holding over the central High Plains beneath the eastward-building ridge. Watch localized flash flooding along the central High Plains frontal corridor and from monsoon storms over Southwest burn scars, slot canyons, and urban areas; the coastal Southeast faces a protracted heavy-rain threat as a slow boundary stalls over the moist airmass. In Canada, the interior stays broadly settled under high pressure and slack gradients across the Prairies, with the active weather confined to the Pacific side — the coastal low and cold front bearing down on British Columbia — and to Atlantic Canada, where tightening isobars near the Gulf of St. Lawrence imply organized lift along the eastern-provinces fronts.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This is the WPC 1200Z surface analysis for 26 August 2026. The dominant high-pressure centers are a 1021 mb high off the mid-Atlantic coast, a 1018 mb high over the central Great Basin, and a 1017 mb high near the upper Great Lakes, none of which are particularly intense for late August and none alone is driving the continental-scale pattern. The most significant low is a system centered near the Pacific Northwest coast around 1000 mb with an associated cold front sweeping southward along the California and Nevada coastline and eastern Pacific, and a separate surface low near 1006 mb over the northern Rockies or high plains with frontal boundaries extending into the central interior. A cold front is draped from that northern Plains low eastward across the upper Midwest, with what appears to be a stationary or slow-moving segment extending into the mid-Mississippi Valley, and a warm front is indicated curving from roughly the upper Great Lakes region toward the Northeast. The tightest pressure gradient is evident across the Pacific Northwest and into British Columbia, where isobars compress around the coastal low, implying the strongest surface winds on this chart; over the southern Plains and much of the Southeast the gradient is slack. Dewpoints in the mid-to-upper 70s F across the Gulf Coast states and lower Mississippi Valley, combined with the frontal boundary positioned across the central Plains to mid-South, identify the primary zone where surface moisture convergence and frontal lift are collocated and where convective potential is most directly supported by the surface pattern alone.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This CMC surface analysis valid 00Z 26 August 2026 shows a broad area of relatively high pressure dominating much of central and western Canada, with an anticenter near 1032 hPa positioned over the central North Pacific and a separate high of around 1024 hPa situated well offshore in the subtropical Pacific, neither of which directly affects the Canadian landmass. Over what appears to be the Canadian Prairies and into the upper Midwest, pressure gradients are comparatively slack between modest ridging and a diffuse trough extending southward, suggesting light and variable surface winds across that corridor. A cluster of low pressure centers in the 993-1003 hPa range occupies the high-latitude portion of the chart, consistent with the Arctic Ocean and Canadian Archipelago rather than the provinces, and should not be read as storm systems threatening populated areas. Along the eastern seaboard and into Atlantic Canada, a series of frontal boundaries and associated lows in the low-1000s hPa are evident, with tightening isobar spacing near the Gulf of St. Lawrence region implying a stronger pressure gradient and the potential for organized lift, though the exact landfall of fronts on the Nova Scotia or Newfoundland coast is difficult to pin precisely at this scale. Tropical Storm Lala is labeled near 35N 177W in the far western Pacific, well outside the Canadian domain and posing no direct threat to the country.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary: Looking at the 500 mb height and temperature analysis valid 1200 UTC 26 August 2026, the dominant feature is a deep longwave trough centered over the upper Midwest and Great Lakes region, with closed height contours around 552-558 dam indicating a cutoff low that has separated from the main westerlies. The ridge axis over the Desert Southwest and Great Basin is marked by the labeled high (H) and heights near 594 dam, creating a high-amplitude ridge-trough couplet with roughly 35-40 dam of amplitude between the western ridge and the eastern trough center. The cutoff low geometry is confirmed by the closed contours and the brown temperature core collocated with the height minimum, indicating a cold-core structure consistent with a self-retaining system that will pivot rather than translate quickly downstream. A secondary trough and implied jet corridor is visible along the Pacific Northwest coast, with another height minimum in that region, and the overall North American pattern appears blocked rather than progressive given the deep cutoff and the anchored western ridge. Winds plotted across the northern plains and Great Lakes region suggest a cyclonic circulation around the cutoff center, while the southern periphery of the system shows flow directed from southwest to northeast across the Mississippi Valley, consistent with a neutral to slightly negative tilt in the trough axis.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary:
Valid 26 Aug 2026 13:41Z, GOES-19 AirMass RGB.

The dominant signal across the central and eastern CONUS is a broad orange-red tone covering the interior from the central Plains southward through Texas and into northern Mexico, indicating dry mid-to-upper tropospheric air consistent with a warm-season ridge centered over that region; this is not a stratospheric intrusion signature but rather the expected dry, subsident character of a summer anticyclone. A sharper, more compact reddish-orange streamer extends from the upper Midwest southeastward toward the Tennessee Valley, wrapping cyclonically on what appears to be the eastern flank of a shortwave trough, and the abrupt color transition along its left edge, running roughly from the Iowa-Illinois area into the central Appalachians, marks the likely jet corridor implied by that airmass boundary. Scattered clusters of bright white high-topped convection are visible along the Atlantic Seaboard from the Carolinas northward into the Mid-Atlantic, as well as an isolated cell near the South Dakota-Nebraska border, both erupting along or near the moisture gradient where green tropical air meets the drier airmass to the west. The Gulf Coast and Florida peninsula show green tones with some shallow convective cells but no organized deep convection, and the Caribbean visible at lower right maintains a moist green signature with a band of moderate cloud near Hispaniola.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary: This GOES-19 Air Mass RGB from 1330Z 26 August 2026 shows a broad green swath across the deep tropics from the eastern Pacific through Central America, the Caribbean, and into equatorial South America, consistent with deep tropical moisture; scattered white high-cloud clusters embedded in this zone over Central America and the western Caribbean suggest active convection, possibly associated with a tropical wave or the eastern Pacific ITCZ. Over Canada, a strong blue-to-red color gradient arching from the northern Canadian Prairies into Quebec and Labrador marks a sharp upper-level airmass boundary, with the blue (cold, dry polar air) to the north and the transition toward orange-red tones to the south implying the implied jet corridor along that boundary. A compact, elongated orange-red feature curves cyclonically off the western Canadian coast and into the Gulf of Alaska, which on the cyclonic flank of an apparent trough is a more credible stratospheric-intrusion or high-PV signature than the broader warm tones sitting over the subtropical ridges. In the South Atlantic, a tight spiral of white cloud near the southeastern Brazilian coast and a broad cloud band sweeping across the Southern Ocean south of Argentina are consistent with an active extratropical cyclone system. The broad orange-red expanse over the subtropical eastern Pacific and subtropical North Atlantic is consistent with dry, subsident air under a summer anticyclonic regime rather than a stratospheric source.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary: The dominant signal on this chart is a broad above-normal temperature probability covering virtually the entire contiguous US east of the Rockies, with the highest confidence centered over central and southern Texas into adjacent Oklahoma and Louisiana, where the 90-100 percent probability class (darkest brown) is plotted. That core grades outward through the 70-80 and 60-70 percent shading across the rest of the southern Plains, the Mississippi Valley, the Southeast, and into the mid-Atlantic and New England, where probabilities drop to the 33-40 percent leaning-above class. The only meaningful below-normal signal in the contiguous US is along coastal and interior California and into the Pacific Northwest, where 50-60 percent odds of below-normal temperatures are depicted, consistent with a persistent or rebuilding trough positioned offshore or over the immediate West Coast. The sharp contrast between the western below-normal and the expansive eastern above-normal signal implies the chart's forecast captures a continued amplified pattern with a western trough and a downstream ridge or ridges dominating the central and eastern US through the early September period, rather than a progressive breakdown into zonal flow. Alaska shows a below-normal center over the Bering Sea region with above-normal odds along the southern mainland, and Hawaii carries a strong above-normal signal at the 70-80 percent level.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary: This is indeed a CPC 6-10 day 500 mb height and height-anomaly forecast, valid 31 August through 4 September 2026, made 25 August 2026. The green solid contours show 500 mb heights at 60 m intervals, with the main ridge axis across the central and eastern contiguous United States near the 588 dam contour, and a prominent closed low centered over the northwestern Canadian interior, approximately over Yukon or adjacent British Columbia, with heights near 528 dam or below at the center. The height anomalies (dashed contours, blue negative and red positive) show a strong negative center of roughly -90 m (about -9 dam) over that northwestern Canadian closed low, while positive anomalies of +40 to +50 m (4-5 dam) persist across the central and southern United States. The zero-anomaly line over western North America runs roughly along the U.S.-Canada border from the Pacific coast eastward, meaning the positive anomaly field has retreated southward and does not extend meaningfully into western Canada; the western U.S. ridge is holding in the southern tier but is not amplified well into the mid-latitudes of western North America. The overall pattern, with a deep trough axis over northwestern Canada tilting toward the Mackenzie Valley and a flattening positive anomaly confined to lower latitudes across the south-central U.S., is consistent with a more amplified meridional flow in the north but a tendency toward zonal or weakly ridged flow across the western U.S. mid-latitudes rather than a sustained high-amplitude western ridge.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary: This chart is a 500 mb heights and anomalies prognostic valid 2–8 September 2026, made 25 August 2026, so it is the CPC 8–14 day product as described. The solid green height contours show a deep, positively tilted trough centered over the Canadian Arctic Archipelago, with the 540 dam contour wrapping tightly around Baffin Island and the adjacent archipelago; contours spread broadly southward across central Canada, placing the main trough axis roughly over Hudson Bay and eastern Canada. Over the contiguous United States the pattern is dominated by a broad ridge: the 570 dam contour covers most of the CONUS south of about 50°N, with the 588 dam contour present across the Desert Southwest and northern Mexico, indicating the ridge core has retreated to the southern Rockies and Southwest rather than remaining over the northern Rockies or northern Plains. The dashed anomaly contours (red positive, blue negative) show a negative anomaly center of roughly 6–9 dam over the Arctic/Baffin region and a broad positive anomaly of 6 dam or more centered over the central and southern CONUS, consistent with a warm, amplified ridge well south of the northern Plains. Western Canada and the northern Rockies sit in a transitional zone between the anomaly centers, with little or no positive anomaly there, confirming the ridge axis has not built into that region.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary:
A strong upper-level ridge maintains extreme heat across the Southwest and South-Central U.S. through Thursday, with highs reaching 100-115 degrees in some areas and dangerous overnight temperatures limiting recovery. Major to Extreme Heat Risk continues across Texas and Southwest.

An eastward-moving upper-level trough drives organized convection along a frontal boundary from the Plains through the Great Lakes and Northeast Wednesday, with heaviest storms across the Mid-Mississippi Valley and Ohio Valley producing large hail, damaging winds, and flash flooding. A slow-moving boundary across the Southeast prolongs heavy rainfall and severe thunderstorm potential through Thursday. Monsoonal moisture supports daily thunderstorms across the Southwest and Rockies with isolated flash flooding threat through Thursday.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary:
SLIGHT RISK area extends from southern Great Lakes/Midwest through central/southern High Plains to Ozarks/Mid-South/Lower Mississippi Valley. Primary threat is damaging winds; large hail also possible, especially central High Plains.

Great Lakes/Midwest: Eastward-moving shortwave trough and surface cold front will trigger isolated to scattered severe storms this afternoon/evening. Multicells and marginal supercells likely; updraft organization aided by 25-35kt deep-layer shear despite modest low-level winds. Brief embedded tornado possible but low hodograph curvature limits tornado risk. Severe threat diminishes evening as convection outpaces instability.

Ozarks/Mid-South/Lower Mississippi Valley: Morning storms tracking south-southeast may strengthen this afternoon across western Tennessee/northern Mississippi as boundary layer destabilizes. Additional afternoon development expected along weak front from southern Missouri into Arkansas/eastern Oklahoma, aided by remnant MCV. Robust downbursts primary threat with multicellular organization.

High Plains: Upslope flow and moderate instability will support supercells and clusters across central High Plains by early afternoon. Both large hail and severe gusts expected, with potential upscale growth into western Kansas evening. Weaker threat farther south across southern High Plains into Oklahoma/Texas Panhandles.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: No active mesoscale discussion. No organized convective threat currently being monitored by SPC.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
ATLANTIC: Tropical wave with low pressure southwest of Cabo Verde Islands (AL96) has disorganized convection. Somewhat favorable conditions over next couple days could support tropical depression formation (60% chance through 48 hours and 7 days), but conditions deteriorate by weekend, limiting longer-term development prospects.

EAST PACIFIC: Active Tropical Storms Lala and Iselle ongoing. System EP93 south of Mexico likely to develop into depression within 24 hours (80% chance 48-hour, 90% chance 7-day) as it moves west-northwest offshore. Broad low east-southeast of Hawaiian Islands has 40% 48-hour chance, 70% 7-day chance of depression formation by late week. Two additional areas have potential for depression development by early next week with lower near-term probabilities.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary: The Oceanic Niño Index shows the equatorial Pacific transitioning from weak La Niña conditions (negative anomalies around -0.6°C in late 2025) toward neutral and then warm phases through spring 2026. The warming trend accelerates from March onward, with anomalies reaching +1.4°C by May-June 2026, indicating a shift toward El Niño conditions. The transition from cold to warm phases occurs primarily during February-April 2026.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary: PNA is weakly negative and falling, with the 7-day mean dropping to -0.70 from -0.29. AO rebounded sharply from negative values early in the period to strongly positive (+0.37 mean) before retreating to -0.35 most recently. NAO has reversed course sharply, collapsing from +0.19 to -0.90 over the past week and now at -1.28. The NAO shift is the most striking signal. Given summer's weak teleconnection regime, these indices provide directional hints rather than strong constraints: PNA's negative bias may offer modest support for troughing patterns, while NAO's recent sharp negative turn could favor a more sluggish Atlantic flow with slower eastward progression of features.
